newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakh oil output stymied by lack of export routes.
newsitem.headline: Kazakh oil output stymied by lack of export routes.

text.p: Oil-rich Kazakhstan will soon have one foot in the door of world energy markets thanks to a dedicated export pipeline project, but it is struggling to get more links built, Western energy sources said on Friday.

Industry sources at an international energy conference said the Caspian Pipeline Consortium's plan to link the Kazakh Tengiz oil field to Russia's Black Sea port near Novorossiisk via a $1.5 billion pipeline was a big step forward.
But they worried that other pipeline proposals were proceeding too slowly.
A lack of multiple oil export pipeline systems has stymied Western energy majors' multi-billion dollar projects which are both producing and planned in Kazakhstan and the Caspian region.

"This (the Caspian link) is one of several pipelines that is going to tie the Caspian region to world markets," said John Keyes, CIS Business Unit Planning Manager at Chevron unit Chevron Overseas Petroleum Inc.
"It's important to note that this line is basically full before it's even built," he said.
Chevron and Mobil, which are developing Kazakhstan's one-billion-tonne Tengiz oil field, are the main customers of the planned Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) link.
The two have had to put the brakes on Tengiz output until the CPC link and other planned routes are built.

But other energy investors planning to tap Kazakhstan's big on- and offshore reserves as well as big deposits in the Azeri sector of the Caspian need new pipelines if they are to get production off the ground.
"The main concern is still the problem of transport to world markets," said Jan Prins, senior vice-president of project finance at ABN-Amro Bank N.V.
Russia, with a strained pipeline system, is unable and unwilling to export more than the 70,000 barrels per day of Kazakh crude it already handles.
That means that international oil producers in Kazakhstan -- which has no direct access to world markets -- are eyeing proposed pipelines through Azerbaijan to Georgia and to Turkey.
But oil sources say there has been little progress in developing a major new route that will carry Azeri and probably Kazakh oil to Turkey's Mediterreanean port of Ceyhan.
"Nothing concrete is going on now (with other pipeline projects)," said a top industry source who declined to be named.
He said plans by a multinational consortium operating in the Azeri sector of the Caspian Sea to build a $1.8 billion link from the Azeri capital Baku to Ceyhan were bogged down in the planning stage.
"The Baku-Batumi line is further along," the executive said, referring to a proposed, smaller pipeline that will link Baku to the Georgian Black Sea port of Batumi.
One option that may need to be retooled is a Kazakh plan for an oil pipeline from its Kumkol field to serve domestic markets.
John Works, a vice-president at JP Morgan, said the Kumkol pipeline was not financeable unless it served export markets. "If they make it an export line, you've got a winner," he said.

Crude oil output in the Caspian region -- including Western Kazakhstan, Western Turkmenistan, Southern Russia, Azerbaijan and Georgia -- will more than triple to 120 million tonnes a year by 2010 from 36.9 million in 1995, according to Nadir Biyikoglu, assistant general manager at Botas Petroleum Pipeline Corp of Turkey.
Kazakhstan says its Caspian continental shelf holds at least 10 billion tonnes of oil, and output there will be at least five million tonnes a year by 2004 and 60 million tonnes a year by 2013.
"Producers must be convinced that uninterrupted transport is guaranteed," Prins said.
